title: The Story of a Tree
directAnswer: Bob makes directed guesses of the form 'u is the parent of v'. Alice picks the root uniformly at random over all n nodes, and Bob wins if at least k guesses turn out correct. The answer is (number of roots that make ≥ k guesses correct) / n, reduced. Compute the correct count for root = 1 with one DFS, then reroot in O(1) per edge: moving the root across edge (u, v) only flips the two guesses on that edge. Count winning roots and reduce the fraction. O(n + g).

remember.pattern: Reroot DP — compute once at root 1, slide the root edge by edge
remember.formula:
guessed = set of directed pairs (a, b) meaning 'a is parent of b'
DFS from root 1:
    base += 1 for every tree edge parent u → child v with (u, v) in guessed
correct[1] = base
reroot (preorder, parent before child):
    for child v of u:
        correct[v] = correct[u]
        if (u, v) in guessed: correct[v] -= 1   # u was parent, no longer
        if (v, u) in guessed: correct[v] += 1   # v becomes parent of u
wins = count of nodes with correct >= k
answer = wins / n  reduced by gcd
rules: A guess (u, v) means **u is the parent of v** — it is **directed**, so store it as an ordered pair, not an unordered edge.
Only the **two guesses living on edge (u, v)** change when the root crosses that edge — every other guess is unaffected. That O(1) update is the whole trick.
Compute `correct[1]` with one DFS, then propagate to every node in **preorder** so each parent's value is ready before its children.
The probability denominator is always **n** (every node is an equally likely root); reduce `wins/n` with `gcd`.
When `wins = 0`, `gcd(0, n) = n`, so the reduced fraction is `0/1` — no special case needed.
whenToUse: An answer is needed for **every possible root** of a tree, not just one fixed root
Re-running an O(n) DFS from each of n roots would be O(n²) and too slow
The quantity at a child differs from its parent's by an **O(1) local correction**
Tree / forest structure where moving the root flips only edge-local state
antiSignals: A single fixed root → one plain DFS, no rerooting
General graph with cycles → rerooting's 'one edge flips' invariant breaks
The per-node answer can't be derived from its parent in O(1) → rerooting gives no speedup
You actually need each root's full subtree recomputed → no shortcut, accept O(n²) or rethink
remember.takeaway: Rerooting turns 'answer this for all n roots' from O(n²) into O(n): solve once at an arbitrary root, then realize that sliding the root over one edge changes only the handful of facts attached to that edge. Here exactly two directed guesses live on each edge, so each move is a ±1 fix.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognize an 'answer for every root' tree problem as a rerooting (re-rooting DP) candidate instead of brute-forcing n separate DFS runs, and whether you correctly treat each guess as a directed parent→child pair.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Treating guesses as undirected edges, recomputing from scratch at each root (O(n²)), or botching the reroot delta — forgetting that crossing edge (u, v) both removes guess (u, v) and adds guess (v, u).
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Derive the O(1) reroot update from first principles ('only edge (u,v)'s two guesses flip'), note the answer is wins/n reduced by gcd, and mention that gcd(0, n) already yields 0/1.

problemStatement:
Alice and Bob play a game on a tree of `n` nodes (labeled `1` to `n`) connected by `n − 1` edges. Alice secretly roots the tree at one node, chosen **uniformly at random** among all `n` nodes. Bob then makes `g` guesses; each guess is a pair `(u, v)` meaning Bob believes **`u` is the parent of `v`** in Alice's rooted tree.

Bob wins if **at least `k`** of his guesses are correct. Return the probability that Bob wins, as a reduced fraction `p/q`.
constraints: edges describe a connected tree (exactly n − 1 edges, no cycles)
0 ≤ g ≤ n − 1 guesses, each a directed pair (u, v)
The answer is a reduced fraction p/q (q > 0)
understanding: The tree is fixed; only the root varies. Each guess (u, v) is a directed claim that u sits immediately above v. For a given root, a guess is correct exactly when v's parent equals u in that rooting. Since the root is uniform over n nodes, the probability Bob wins is (count of roots producing ≥ k correct guesses) / n. The key structural fact: as the root moves from one endpoint of an edge to the other, only the guesses that lie on that very edge can change their truth value — guess (u, v) is correct while the root is on u's side and wrong once the root crosses to v's side, and vice versa for guess (v, u).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is a guess directed — does (u, v) mean u is the parent of v, or just that u and v are adjacent?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Directed: u is the parent of v. (v, u) is a different guess. They must be stored as ordered pairs.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the root chosen uniformly at random?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — each of the n nodes is equally likely, so the denominator of the probability is n.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Could the same guess appear twice, or could both (u, v) and (v, u) be guessed?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Both directions of an edge may be guessed; each is counted independently. I store them in a set of ordered pairs so each contributes once.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What is returned when no root makes Bob win?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: 0/1 — the reduced form of 0/n. gcd(0, n) = n handles this automatically.

examples.explanation: Roots 1 and 3 make both guesses correct (≥ 2); roots 2 and 4 make only 1 correct. Wins = 2 of 4 → 2/4 = 1/2.
Guess '1 is parent of 2' holds when root ∈ {1, 3} (root 1: 2's parent is 1; root 3: path 3-1-2 still makes 1 the parent of 2). Root 2 makes 1 a child of 2 → wrong. Wins = 2 of 3.
Root 1: 1 is parent of 2 → correct. Root 2: 2 is parent of 1 → guess wrong. Wins = 1 of 2.

diagrams.title: Choosing rerooting over brute force
diagrams.caption: Needing an answer at every root, with an O(1) parent→child delta, is the rerooting signal.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Re-root From Every Node
approaches.whenToMention: State this first to frame the problem: 'the literal reading is — try each of the n roots, count correct guesses, tally winners'. Then explain why O(n²) is too slow at n = 10⁵.
hints: The probability is (winning roots) / n. What is the most direct way to know whether a specific root is a winner?
Fix a root, run a DFS/BFS that records each node's parent, then count how many guesses (u, v) satisfy 'parent of v == u'. Repeat for all n roots.
Each root costs O(n + g); doing it n times is O(n·(n + g)) — correct but quadratic. Use it to validate the fast solution on small inputs.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each root requires a full traversal O(n) plus checking g guesses O(g). Running that for all n possible roots gives O(n · (n + g)). With n up to 10⁵ this is ~10¹⁰ operations — far too slow, but conceptually simple and a perfect correctness oracle.
approaches.explanation:
The definition of the answer is operational, so the brute force just executes the definition.

**The loop.** For every candidate root `r` from 1 to n: traverse the tree from `r`, assigning each visited node its parent in that rooting. Then scan all `g` guesses; a guess `(u, v)` is correct iff the parent recorded for `v` equals `u`. If the number of correct guesses is `≥ k`, increment `wins`.

**Why it is correct.** It computes, for each root, exactly the quantity the problem defines — the count of correct guesses — and compares it to `k`. Nothing is approximated. This makes it the ideal oracle to diff against the optimized version on random small trees.

**Why we don't ship it.** Re-traversing the whole tree from scratch for each of the n roots throws away an enormous amount of shared structure: most parent relationships are identical between adjacent roots. That redundancy is exactly what the rerooting solution exploits. At n = 10⁵, O(n²) is hopeless; mention this approach, then improve it.
approaches.insight: Brute force here is the specification made executable. Its weakness — recomputing nearly-identical parent maps n times — points directly at the optimization: when the root moves to a neighbor, almost nothing changes.

pitfalls: Treating a guess as undirected — (u, v) and (v, u) are different claims.
Re-allocating visited[] and recomputing for all n roots — accepted only as an oracle, never as the final answer at n = 10⁵.
Forgetting to reduce the fraction with gcd.

approaches.name: Rerooting DP (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The intended solution. Phrase it as 'solve once at root 1, then slide the root one edge at a time, fixing only the two guesses on each crossed edge in O(1)'.
hints: Brute force recomputes almost the same parent map for every root. When the root moves from u to an adjacent v, which guesses can possibly change their correctness?
Only the guesses on the edge (u, v). Guess (u, v) ('u parent of v') was correct while rooted on u's side and is wrong once v is the root's side; guess (v, u) flips the other way.
Compute correct[1] with one DFS. Then BFS/DFS outward: correct[child] = correct[parent] − [ (parent,child) guessed ] + [ (child,parent) guessed ]. Count nodes with correct ≥ k.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Building the adjacency list and guess set is O(n + g). The first DFS is O(n). The reroot pass visits each node once and does O(1) work per edge → O(n). Counting winners is O(n). Total O(n + g), with O(n + g) space for the adjacency list, guess set, and per-node arrays.
approaches.explanation:
The brute force is wasteful because adjacent roots share nearly all parent relationships. Rerooting computes the answer once and then transports it across the tree.

**Step 1 — anchor at root 1.** One DFS from node 1 records each node's parent and counts `base`: the number of guesses `(u, v)` where `u` is the parent of `v` in this rooting. Set `correct[1] = base`.

**Step 2 — the reroot delta.** Consider an edge between `u` (already settled, root on its side) and its child `v`. Imagine physically moving the root from `u`'s side to `v`'s side. Every guess except those *on this edge* keeps the same parent→child orientation, so its correctness is unchanged. Only two guesses can flip:
- `(u, v)` — 'u is parent of v' — was correct (root on u's side) and becomes wrong → subtract 1 if it was guessed.
- `(v, u)` — 'v is parent of u' — was wrong and becomes correct → add 1 if it was guessed.

So `correct[v] = correct[u] − [(u,v) guessed] + [(v,u) guessed]`.

**Why only that edge changes.** Re-rooting from `u` to `v` reverses the direction of exactly one edge in the rooted tree — the `u–v` edge. Every other edge keeps the same parent and child, so every other guess's truth value is untouched. That locality is the entire reason the update is O(1).

**Step 3 — propagate and tally.** Process nodes in preorder (parent before child) so each `correct[u]` is final before its children read it. After filling `correct[]` for all n nodes, count how many satisfy `correct[node] ≥ k`; that is `wins`. Return `wins / n` reduced by `gcd` (and `gcd(0, n) = n` already gives `0/1`).
approaches.insight: Re-rooting reverses exactly one edge's parent/child relationship per move, so any quantity that decomposes over edges updates in O(1). Here each edge carries at most two directed guesses, making the delta a clean ±1. This 'compute once, slide everywhere' template recurs in 'Sum of Distances in Tree' and many tree-DP problems.

dryRun.intro: guessed = {(1,2),(3,4)}. DFS from 1 first, then slide the root outward, fixing only each crossed edge.

steps.action: nodes with correct ≥ 2: node 1 and node 3

code.python:
from math import gcd

def story_of_a_tree(self, n: int, edges: list[list[int]], guesses: list[list[int]], k: int) -> str:
    adj: list[list[int]] = [[] for _ in range(n + 1)]
    for u, v in edges:
        adj[u].append(v)
        adj[v].append(u)
    guessed = {(a, b) for a, b in guesses}        # directed pairs
    parent = [0] * (n + 1)
    visited = [False] * (n + 1)
    order: list[int] = []
    base = 0
    stack = [1]
    visited[1] = True
    while stack:
        u = stack.pop()
        order.append(u)
        for v in adj[u]:
            if not visited[v]:
                visited[v] = True
                parent[v] = u
                if (u, v) in guessed:
                    base += 1
                stack.append(v)
    correct = [0] * (n + 1)
    correct[1] = base
    for u in order:                               # preorder: parent before child
        for v in adj[u]:
            if parent[v] == u:                    # v is a child of u
                c = correct[u]
                if (u, v) in guessed:
                    c -= 1                         # u no longer parent of v
                if (v, u) in guessed:
                    c += 1                         # v becomes parent of u
                correct[v] = c
    wins = sum(1 for node in range(1, n + 1) if correct[node] >= k)
    g = gcd(wins, n)
    return f"{wins // g}/{n // g}"

java.explanation: Order-preserving encoding so (u,v) and (v,u) are distinct keys.
Counts guesses already correct when the tree is rooted at node 1.

java.line: if (parent[v] == u) {                 // v is a child of u
java.explanation: Identifies the rooted-at-1 children; reversing this edge is the only change when the root moves to v.

java.line: if (guessed.contains((long) u * (n + 1) + v)) c--;   // u no longer parent of v
java.explanation: The guess that u parents v was correct on u's side and breaks once v is the root's side.

java.line: if (guessed.contains((long) v * (n + 1) + u)) c++;   // v becomes parent of u
java.explanation: The reverse guess becomes correct after the root crosses to v.

python.line: guessed = {(a, b) for a, b in guesses}        # directed pairs

python.explanation: Correct guesses under the initial root-at-1 orientation.

python.line: for u in order:                               # preorder: parent before child
python.explanation: Guarantees correct[u] is final before any child reads it.

python.line:
if (u, v) in guessed:
                    c -= 1                         # u no longer parent of v
python.explanation: Remove the guess that flips from right to wrong as the root crosses the edge.

python.line:
if (v, u) in guessed:
                    c += 1                         # v becomes parent of u
python.explanation: Add the guess that flips from wrong to right.

diagrams.caption: Start with correct[1] from the DFS, then each child inherits its parent's value ± the edge's two guesses.

edgeCases.behavior: correct[node] = 0 for all roots; if k ≥ 1 then wins = 0 → 0/1. If k = 0 every root wins → 1/1 (but k ≥ 1 per constraints).

edgeCases.input: Both (u,v) and (v,u) guessed on one edge
edgeCases.behavior: Crossing the edge does −1 and +1 simultaneously — net 0 — which is correct, since exactly one of the two is always right.
Single node, no edges, no guesses; wins = (k ≤ 0 ? 1 : 0). With k ≥ 1, answer is 0/1.

pitfalls: Processing children before parents — use preorder so correct[parent] is final first.
Forgetting the +1 for the reverse guess (v, u) when crossing an edge.
Encoding guesses as unordered edges, collapsing (u, v) and (v, u).
Recursive DFS at n = 10⁵ risking stack overflow — use an explicit stack.

commonMistakes: Treating each guess as an undirected edge instead of a directed parent→child claim.
Brute-forcing a fresh DFS from every root (O(n²)) at n = 10⁵.
Botching the reroot delta — applying −1 for (u,v) but forgetting +1 for (v,u).
Returning an unreduced fraction, or mishandling the wins = 0 case.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Undirected guess
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A guess (u, v) asserts u is the parent of v. Storing it as an unordered edge makes (v, u) look guessed too, double-counting correctness and corrupting the reroot delta.
commonMistakesDetailed.good: guessed = {(a, b) for a, b in guesses}   # ordered: a is parent of b

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Incomplete reroot delta
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Crossing edge (u, v) flips two guesses: (u, v) goes right→wrong and (v, u) goes wrong→right. Applying only the −1 undercounts every root on v's side.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Recomputing per root
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Re-running a DFS from each of n roots is O(n²). At n = 10⁵ it times out; rerooting reuses the root-1 computation and slides it in O(1) per edge.

followupVariations.title: Sum of Distances in Tree
followupVariations.hint: Classic rerooting: compute distances from one root, then slide — answer[child] = answer[parent] − subtreeSize[child] + (n − subtreeSize[child]).

followupVariations.title: Tree Distances / Maximum Depth From Every Node
followupVariations.hint: Two DFS passes (down then up) propagate the farthest distance to every node — the same compute-once-then-reroot idea.

followupVariations.title: Count Subtrees / Rerooting Aggregates
followupVariations.hint: Any edge-decomposable aggregate (sums, counts, max) can be rerooted in O(n) once the O(1) parent→child delta is known.

patternNote: Canonical Rerooting (Re-rooting DP). Recognize it whenever a tree problem asks for an answer at every node/root and the child's answer differs from the parent's by an O(1), edge-local correction. Solve once at an arbitrary root, then propagate. Here each edge holds at most two directed guesses, so the delta is a clean ±1.
